paras: The killing of Wm. Bowie was the fatal shooting of a Black steamboat roustabout by Shreveport, Louisiana, policeman E. C. McRady in late September or early October 1881, after Bowie was accused of shooting Aaron White, a Black man helping the officer make an arrest. According to the Shreveport Standard, McRady fired his rifle when Bowie advanced on him with a cocked pistol and refused to drop it. Louisiana state-news columns called Bowie a "colored desperado" and reported that McRady had been "exonerated from blame."

The trouble began in a saloon behind the Red store at the head of Milam street, a place the Standard called a "den" and "an intolerable nuisance." There Eliza Jackson, described by the paper as "a colored woman of bad repute," had words with Bowie and asked McRady, the policeman on the beat, to arrest him for being disorderly and abusing her. McRady took Bowie by the arm and told him he was under arrest.

Abe Johnson, another Black man in the room, then interfered, declaring that "there wasn't policemen enough in Shreveport to arrest him." McRady let go of Bowie and grappled with Johnson, calling on two Black men, Elbridge Geary and Aaron White, to help; Johnson threw Geary aside and, in the Standard's telling, urged Bowie to take the officer's pistol and shoot him. Bowie, the paper said, snatched the pistol from McRady's hip pocket and pointed it at him, then turned and fired at White, who was running away. Dr. Booth cut the ball out under White's left arm, and he was said to be doing as well as could be expected.

Bowie and Johnson escaped through the back gate and the hollow toward the Charity Hospital, while McRady went to the station house, armed himself and set out in pursuit with J. R. Herndon. The printed text of the Standard's account has a gap at this point, so the coverage does not show where or how the pursuers overtook Bowie. When the account resumes, Bowie had turned the pistol on McRady, who twice ordered him to drop it; as Bowie kept advancing, McRady fired his Whitney rifle and killed him "almost instantly." Bowie fell with the cocked pistol, a Tranter, in his hand, and the Standard remarked that McRady and Herndon were lucky he "did not know how to use it."

The Standard said its facts had been "established before the Mayor's court" the morning after, where Johnson described the scuffle in his own words. Johnson was later charged with assault with intent to murder McRady and White "on the 26th," and Constable Murray arrested him in the city lockup on that state charge. Judge S. L. Taylor then ordered Sheriff Lake to return the prisoner to the city authorities until he had served a sentence already imposed by the Mayor's Court.

On October 15 the Donaldsonville Chief reported that McRady, who it said had killed Bowie "in self defense," had been exonerated, without naming the body that cleared him. No report of an inquest appears in the coverage, which also does not show whether White recovered.

All of the coverage came from white papers and rested on the officer's side of the encounter. The Louisiana Capitolian of Baton Rouge reprinted the Standard's long account under the headline "Shot Dead in His Tracks" on October 6 and again on October 8. The Standard printed the curses attributed to Johnson and Bowie in full and called White "a well known colored boy, an employee of the barber-shops."

The Donaldsonville Chief's state-news column of October 8 condensed the story to two sentences, calling Bowie "a vicious and desperate colored malefactor who resisted arrest and tried to shoot the officer." A week later the same column labeled him "a colored desperado" in reporting McRady's exoneration. Outside Louisiana, the South Kentuckian of Hopkinsville gave the killing a single line on October 11, describing Bowie as "a negro" who "resisted arrest."

The Capitolian also reprinted the Shreveport Times item on Judge Taylor's order in Johnson's case on October 11 and October 15, under the heading "Important Decision," as a ruling on the city's power to enforce its ordinances.
